issues.legal_issue: Limiting the succession rights of heirs of a deceased statutory tenant of residential premises, while allowing broader succession rights for commercial premises, does not deny equal protection when the two kinds of tenancy have materially different characteristics and the distinction bears a reasonable relation to the legislative purpose.
material_facts: The challenged rule limited which family members of a deceased statutory tenant of residential premises could continue in possession and, in specified circumstances, limited the period of that possession.
The rule did not impose the same limits on heirs of statutory tenants of commercial premises.
The petitioners, as heirs of deceased statutory tenants of residential premises, challenged the different treatment as discriminatory.

The Court relied on the distinct characteristics of commercial tenancies, including that a tenant's business premises may be the source of livelihood for the tenant and family, and that a running business may be a valuable family asset.
issues.conclusion: The limits on succession to residential statutory tenancies were not discriminatory and did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits reasonable classification based on an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object of the law; it requires equal treatment of persons similarly situated, not identical treatment of distinct categories. The Court applied the tests stated in Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar, drawing on Budhan Choudhry v. State of Bihar, and the equality principles stated in Western U.P. Electric Power & Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P. It relied on Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar for the distinct treatment and features of residential and commercial tenancies, and on Sakhawat Ali v. State of Orissa for the principle that a legislature may choose which categories to include in legislation. The protection of a tenant and successors after termination of tenancy is created by legislation, and the legislature may set its extent and manner.

rule.if: equality_validity_challenge and deceased_residential_statutory_tenant and succession_rights_are_limited and residential_and_commercial_tenancies_have_distinct_features and commercial_premises_support_business_livelihood

predicates.equality_validity_challenge: Heirs challenged a rule limiting succession to a deceased tenant's residential tenancy as unequal treatment.
predicates.deceased_residential_statutory_tenant: A person whose residential tenancy had ended died while continuing in possession under statutory protection.
predicates.succession_rights_are_limited: The governing rule limited the family members entitled to continue in possession and imposed conditions or time limits on that entitlement.
predicates.residential_and_commercial_tenancies_hav: The dispute involved different succession treatment for residential and commercial tenancies, which the Court treated as distinct categories.
predicates.commercial_premises_support_business_liv: A tenant's commercial premises could support a business that provided the tenant and the tenant's family with their livelihood.

issues.definition: When heirs challenge limits on succession to a deceased tenant's residential tenancy, and residential and commercial tenancies have distinct features including the livelihood role of commercial premises, those limits do not violate equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: Limiting the succession rights of heirs of a deceased statutory tenant of residential premises does not violate the constitutional protection of life and personal liberty merely because the limitation may require the heirs to leave the premises.
material_facts: The petitioners, as heirs of deceased statutory tenants of residential premises, challenged restrictions on their ability to continue in possession after the tenant's death.
The restrictions limited the eligible successors and, in specified circumstances, the duration of their possession.
The petitioners argued that the right to shelter under Article 21 was infringed by limiting the heirs' rights.
The Court regarded the protection of a tenant and successors after termination of tenancy as a statutory benefit whose nature and extent could be set by the legislature.
issues.conclusion: The challenged limits on the heirs' rights did not violate Article 21; the Court held that the restrictions were reasonable, fair and just in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 does not prevent the legislature from defining the nature and extent of statutory protection for successors to a tenant whose tenancy has ended. The Court rejected the argument that the asserted right to shelter made the limits on succession to residential statutory tenancies unconstitutional, and held that those limits were reasonable, fair and just in the circumstances.

rule.if: shelter_right_validity_challenge and deceased_residential_statutory_tenant and succession_rights_are_limited and statutory_tenancy_protection_is_legislatively_created

predicates.shelter_right_validity_challenge: Heirs argued that limits on their ability to remain in residential premises infringed the constitutional protection of life and personal liberty because it includes shelter.
predicates.deceased_residential_statutory_tenant: A person whose residential tenancy had ended died while continuing in possession under statutory protection.
predicates.succession_rights_are_limited: The governing rule limited the family members entitled to continue in possession and imposed conditions or time limits on that entitlement.
predicates.statutory_tenancy_protection_is_legislat: The protection allowing a tenant or successor to remain after termination of a tenancy arose from legislation.

issues.definition: When heirs challenge limits on succession to a deceased tenant's residential tenancy on the basis of shelter, and the tenancy protection is legislatively created, those limits do not violate the shelter right.
